label: verify-bm-passive-facades-evidence

claims.claim: No measured energy, comfort or daylight benefit exists for humidity-driven passive facade shading; the Freiburg study measured shade coverage only (50-90% in summer) and defers the indoor benefit to future work.
claims.source_says: While we have focused on evaluating the 4D-printed shading elements through analysis of shade coverage in this study, it will be important to quantify the improvement of indoor climate regulation in future work.
claims.note: The Freiburg part and the 50-90% shade coverage are confirmed in Cheng 2024, but the sweeping 'none exists anywhere' is an absence claim from a limited search that no source can support.

claims.claim: Relative humidity is only an indirect proxy for shade need; works in dry-summer climates, authors leave humid tropics untested; own calculation shows Singapore element mostly open in 98% of shade-wanted hours, weak in Houston, Mumbai, Sydney.
claims.source_says: temperate climate with dry and hot summers as well as humid and cold winters, creating an indirect but reliable link between the need for shading and the behavior of hygromorphic materials in response to RH
claims.note: Cheng quote and the tropical-untested statement are verbatim in the paper; the saved script output shows Singapore 0.98, Houston 0.38, Mumbai 0.43, Sydney 0.50 (I read the saved JSON, did not re-run, as the script writes into the other agent's folders).

claims.claim: Humidity-controlled ventilation is the only passive humidity-responsive element with in-service numbers: 30% airflow cut in occupied Paris dwellings vs constant-flow reference (manufacturer); independent simulation 14-27% heating saving; fails on upper floors of tall blocks without fans.
claims.source_says: The measured savings on the airflow for this project have been evaluated at 30% in average (55% if extrapolating to the statistical average occupancy in France). / System C+ allows to increase the energy savings up to 27% ... and 14% for ... average airtightness.
claims.note: The 30%, 14-27% and upper-floor ineffectiveness (Sowa abstract, simulation) all reproduce, but 'the only' element with in-service numbers is an unverifiable universal and the manufacturer authorship was not checked by me.

claims.claim: Durability evidence for any passive responsive facade element is short: 170 lab cycles and 13 months (cellulose bilayer), days (wax tile), 264 hours (hydrogel window); none approaches building lifetime.
claims.source_says: The number of cycles tested is still small compared to the entire lifetime of a building ... lost its thermochromic function after 264 hours of continuous operation due to water evaporation
claims.note: 170 cycles, 13 months and 264 h are confirmed, but the wax tile paper only says tests were done in July and September, so 'days' is not stated, and 'any element' overgeneralises.

overall: Three of four key claims are accurate on the specifics I could check against the original papers (Cheng 2024, Aereco/AIVC paper, Van den Bossche 2007, Sowa 2020 abstract, Yang 2025, arXiv 2308.01530). Each also carries a universal 'no' or 'only' that no source supports, plus one wax-tile duration ('days') the paper does not give. The RH-versus-shade numbers match the agent's saved output, but I did not re-run the script because it writes into the agent's own folders.
